message.reasoning:
I need to decide on a Monopoly action.

I have $785 and three unmortgaged pink properties with no houses. No monopolies exist yet. Player 1 has cash and several reds but lacks Indiana.

Player 2 has a dark blue monopoly with four houses each and a get-out-of-jail-free card. Player 4 is nearly broke with only seventeen dollars and a light blue monopoly. Player 1 lacks Indiana, so he cannot complete the red set.

Player 2 will not sell Virginia. I cannot complete the pink set or build a brown monopoly. I am deciding between ending my turn, proposing a trade, or mortgaging a property.

Player 1 cannot complete any major set either. Player 4 is nearly bankrupt, so any trade must avoid giving player 2 cash or properties that would help him build hotels on his dark blue monopoly.

Player 2 can already afford hotels on his dark blue set. Player 4's light blue properties are dangerous: Connecticut at four houses costs $450, and a hotel would be $600. I can survive one hit but not two.

Player 4 cannot unmortgage his light blue properties because he lacks the cash. Trading with him would not help me complete a set, and he is unlikely to sell his monopoly for any benefit.

Player 2 might trade Virginia for my pink properties. That would complete the pink monopoly. Player 2 already owns a dark blue monopoly and has no pink set. Virginia is just a dead deed to them.

A pink monopoly would cost $900 for three houses on each property. I only have $785, so two houses per property would leave me with $185. Player 2 knows that giving me a pink set would be dangerous.

Player 2 would not trade Virginia cheaply. A pink monopoly with two houses costs only $150 each, which is not lethal to them, but three houses would hurt them badly. Player 4 has no railroads to offer, and he will not sell his light blue monopoly.

I just paid fifty dollars to get out of jail. I am now on New York Avenue and will circle the board. Dark blue is only a few rolls away. I must avoid landing there.

Four houses on Park Place or Boardwalk would cost $1,300. That is more than double my cash, so I would go bankrupt instantly if I land there.

The only ways to survive are completing a set and building fast, or hoping another player bankrupts Player 2 before I hit his dark blue set. Player 4's light blue properties could force that bankruptcy.

Player 2 is on Pennsylvania Avenue and will pass the light blue properties before reaching dark blue. I am about eighteen spaces from Park Place, which means two to three rolls at average speed. I could land there before Player 2 returns.

I could reach dark blue in as few as two rolls, or by drawing a Community Chest or Chance card. Player 2 will likely refuse any trade for Virginia because a pink monopoly would kill them. I cannot complete an orange, red, or yellow set through pairwise trades alone.

I am now considering a two-step trade. First I would acquire Player 4's mortgaged yellow properties, then take Marvin from Player 1. Player 4 is nearly broke and might sell those mortgaged deeds for cash to survive. I need to check whether receiving mortgaged property in this game requires paying interest immediately or can be deferred.

Player 1 wants six hundred dollars for Marvin. Player 4 has the other two mortgaged yellows but cannot unmortgage them without cash. Player 1 cannot complete the yellow set without Player 4. Player 4 cannot unmortgage without money. This leaves the yellow set in a stalemate.

The green set is impossible to complete because North Carolina is unowned and Player 2 already holds Pennsylvania Avenue. The red set would require buying all three properties, which is expensive. Player 1 might sell Kentucky and Illinois for cash, but Indiana remains with Player 2.

Player 2 will not trade New York Avenue for railroads. Player 1 could complete the orange set with it, so Player 2 is unlikely to give it up. Player 4 is only seventeen dollars away from bankruptcy and cannot unmortgage his light blue properties.

Bankrupting Player 4 would remove the light blue threat, but his properties would be auctioned and Player 2 could buy them. I cannot bankrupt him because his properties do not cost enough to threaten me. I am now considering offering cash plus Baltic Avenue for Virginia from Player 2.

A cash offer for Virginia would leave too little money to build. Two houses on the pink properties cost $150 each, which is not enough to threaten Player 2 or Player 1. Three houses require $900, so mortgaging my pink properties would be necessary. Their combined mortgage value is only $170.

Mortgaging a property prevents building on that set, so I cannot mortgage Virginia and still construct houses there. A three-house pink monopoly would cost $900, which is impossible with my current cash. Two houses per property would cost $600, leaving me with only about $185 after the trade. That is not enough to threaten Player 2. Even paying up to $85 for a partial set would not bankrupt them quickly.

A cash buffer is an illusion against the dark blue threat. Player 2 already holds the winning position and wants me and others to go bankrupt to them. They will reject any trade that creates a pink monopoly unless it gives them something far more valuable.

Player 2 can survive one light blue hit, so he is not desperate to trade for a pink monopoly. Player 1 owns two railroads and red properties, but he would only want cash from me, which I do not want to give.

A two-step trade for the red set is possible. Player 1 might sell Kentucky and Illinois for cash, then take Indiana from Player 2. Player 1 is cash-poor and wants to complete a set, so he may accept that deal. I can only propose one trade this turn.

Player 4 is on the B&O railroad and has only seventeen dollars. He cannot unmortgage his light blue properties without cash, so he might sell them for fifty to one hundred dollars each. Buying Pacific would not complete a set, and buying Atlantic plus Ventnor still requires Marvin from Player 1. Player 1 previously rejected a forty-five-hundred-dollar offer for Marvin, so I would need to pay six hundred dollars to acquire it. That would leave me with only one hundred eighty-five dollars, which is too little to unmortgage the two yellows afterward.

I will propose a trade to Player 4 for Atlantic and Ventnor. I will offer about eighty dollars cash. Player 4 has only seventeen dollars and cannot unmortgage these properties. After the trade I would have roughly seven hundred five dollars left.

Unmortgaging the two yellows would cost $297, leaving only about $408. That is still short of the $600 needed for Marvin. Even if I sold my pink properties for $170, I would have roughly $375 left, which is not enough to cover the unmortgage cost. I cannot build any houses on the yellows with that remaining cash.

The yellow set is too expensive this turn and would not immediately threaten anyone. Player 1 might refuse to sell Marvin because it blocks the yellow set. Player 2 might also reject trading Indiana for cash, since they want to block Player 1 from completing a red monopoly.

Aggressive trades are too risky. I will end my turn and preserve my seven hundred eighty-five dollars. I am watching for an unowned Mediterranean Avenue to complete a brown monopoly with Baltic Avenue. Even with hotels, the combined rent is only four hundred fifty dollars, which is not enough to bankrupt Player 2 in one hit. It could still hurt Player 1 or Player 4.

I will not trade Baltic Avenue away. I need to preserve cash to buy the unowned Mediterranean Avenue for sixty dollars when I land there, then build houses. Reaching it from New York Avenue requires passing Go and landing on space one, which is twenty-two spaces away. That is possible in three turns, though no Chance card sends me directly there. North Carolina is also unowned at space thirty-two, but I currently own no green properties.

I will skip North Carolina because it does not complete a set and would drain my cash buffer. I am now considering whether any single trade this turn could actually help me, but every option seems unworkable.

Player 2 already has four houses on dark blue and $679, so they will likely hotel next turn. I cannot trade to reduce their rent.

I am weighing whether to propose a deceptive trade. The rules say the engine applies the action and updates the state, then asks again if more post-turn actions remain legal. This suggests the turn might continue after a rejected offer, or the trade could simply wait for the opponent's response.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

messages.content:
You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.
